scenes.heading: Real-Time Go: WebSockets & SSE
scenes.narration: Real-time delivery in Go starts with two mechanisms: full-duplex WebSockets and one-way Server-Sent Events. Let's see when to reach for each.

scenes.heading: Two transports, two shapes
items: WebSockets: full-duplex, born from an HTTP Upgrade handshake
SSE: one-way server-to-client over a normal HTTP response
SSE auto-reconnects and passes proxies unchanged
scenes.narration: A WebSocket is a full-duplex connection born from an HTTP Upgrade handshake, so the same socket then speaks the WebSocket frame protocol. Server-Sent Events need no upgrade at all: you keep a normal text-event-stream response open and flush framed events. SSE is one-directional, auto-reconnects in the browser's EventSource, and traverses proxies and load balancers unchanged.

scenes.text: gorilla/websocket allows at most ONE concurrent reader and ONE concurrent writer per connection.
scenes.narration: Here is the rule that shapes everything. The gorilla WebSocket library permits at most one concurrent reader and one concurrent writer per connection. Two goroutines writing to the same connection is a data race that corrupts the frame stream and panics with concurrent write to websocket connection. This is exactly why real-time Go code is structured as separate read and write pumps.

scenes.heading: The hub & broadcast pattern
scenes.narration: To serve many clients you funnel everything through a single hub goroutine that owns three channels: register, unregister, and broadcast. Because only this one goroutine ever touches the client map, no mutexes are needed. A broadcast simply ranges over the clients and pushes onto each one's buffered send channel — and if a client is too slow, the hub drops it rather than blocking everyone else.

scenes.heading: Keeping connections healthy
steps: The writePump sends periodic ping frames
Each incoming pong resets a read deadline
No pong in time means ReadMessage errors out
The dead connection is torn down and reclaimed
scenes.narration: TCP will happily keep a dead connection open for minutes, so WebSocket apps use control frames. The write pump sends periodic pings, and each incoming pong resets a read deadline through a pong handler. If no pong arrives before the deadline, ReadMessage returns an error and the connection is torn down, reclaiming its goroutines and memory — essential to stop a long-lived server from leaking clients.

scenes.text: Use SSE for one-way feeds; reserve WebSockets for truly bidirectional traffic; fan out with Redis pub/sub.
scenes.narration: So reach for SSE when you only push updates one way — live scores, notifications, or LLM token streams — since it's simpler and cheaper. Reserve WebSockets for genuinely bidirectional traffic like chat or multiplayer. And to scale either across instances, put a Redis pub/sub layer between them so a message on one instance reaches clients on the others.
